title: Friction and wheels
summary: Drag a loaded block over three surfaces with the spring scale, then pull the robot's own wheels over the same surfaces, and compare sliding against rolling.
materials: a small wooden or plastic block with a screw-eye hook
a fixed load to put on the block (books or washers)
mBot v1.2, batteries out so it rolls free
three household surfaces (carpet, bare floor, a towel or rubber mat)

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, same as every week: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: why does the robot roll on wheels instead of sliding on skis? Something resists motion when two surfaces touch, and it resists sliding far more than it resists rolling.

Imagine: a block dragged flat across a floor fights to keep touching it the whole way. A wheel touches the floor at one small point at a time and rolls that point forward instead of scraping it.

Plan: pick three surfaces around the house that feel clearly different underfoot, from slippery to grippy. Test the same loaded block on all three with the spring scale, then test the robot's wheels on the same three. Keep the load and the pulling speed the same every time, so only the surface changes.

figure.alt: On the left, a block dragged across the ground touches it along its whole flat face, a wide contact that friction resists strongly. On the right, a wheel touches the ground at one small patch, which is why rolling needs far less pulling force than sliding the same load.

steps.title: Friction resists sliding
steps.body:
Friction is the force that resists two surfaces sliding past each other. It comes from how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together, and from very little else. A wide block and a narrow block of the same weight need close to the same pull force, even though the wide one looks like it touches more.

Rolling is a different kind of touching. A wheel meets the ground at one small patch, and that patch barely slides at all. It mostly just presses and lifts away as the wheel turns. That is why wheels typically need far less force to move the same load than dragging it flat, often by ten times or more.

The robot's wheels still have some friction working for them, not against them. Without any grip at all, the wheels would spin in place and the robot would go nowhere. Friction is not always the enemy, and this week you measure both faces of it.

figure.alt: The spring scale pulls the loaded block across a surface on the left, and pulls the mBot with its wheels rolling free across the same surface on the right, both read at the moment motion starts.

steps.title: Drag the block, then pull the wheels
steps.body:
Load the block with the same books or washers for the whole test and hook the spring scale to its screw eye. On each surface, pull it slowly and steadily and read the force at the moment it starts to slide, not after it is already moving. Test all three surfaces this way.

Then take the batteries out of the mBot so its wheels turn freely, and hook the spring scale to its frame. Pull it slowly across the same three surfaces, same start-to-slide reading. Keep the pulling speed as close to the same as you can manage on every pull, since a faster yank always reads higher.

Read each surface three times for the block and three times for the robot, and use the middle reading each time.
checklist: The same load stayed on the block for every surface, nothing added or removed between pulls
All three surfaces tested for both the block and the robot's wheels
Every pull was slow and steady, and the reading was taken right as motion started
The wheels needed less force than the block on every surface tested

steps.title: Surface versus pull force
steps.body:
The load, the pulling speed and the three surfaces stay the same for both the block and the robot. Only the object being pulled changes between the two numeric columns.

Test three surfaces, three runs each, nine rows in total. For each run, write the surface, the block's pull force in newtons, and the robot's pull force in newtons on that same surface.
steps.question: On which surface was the gap between the block and the wheels the biggest, and by about how many newtons?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each surprise. Classics this week: a jerky pull that reads higher than a true sliding force, and a surface that was not quite clean or flat enough for a fair pull.

Also watch for the robot's wheels catching on carpet fibres instead of rolling, which can make carpet read closer to the block than expected.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the loaded block being pulled by the spring scale on the grippiest surface, next to the robot being pulled the same way on the same surface, and your graph paper table with all nine rows
